query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Polycrystalline copper with a refined grain structure exhibits enhanced ductility at ambient conditions because its FCC crystal structure enables multiple slip systems and efficient dislocation motion.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional coarse-grained polycrystalline copper with a typical FCC structure
generation.intervention: Thermomechanical processing to achieve controlled grain refinement and optimize stacking fault energy
generation.conditions: Ambient (room temperature) deformation conditions typical of mechanical testing
generation.structural_mediator: Grain size reduction that minimizes stress concentrations and facilitates uniform dislocation glide along the multiple slip systems in the FCC structure
generation.mechanism: The intrinsic FCC crystal structure of copper provides many slip systems which, when combined with grain refinement, reduces barriers to dislocation movement and delays localized stress buildup, resulting in improved ductility
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to coarse-grained copper, the grain-refined copper is expected to exhibit a higher uniform elongation and improved ductility without a significant loss in strength under ambient conditions
generation.boundary: The ductility enhancement might be diminished or behave differently under extreme temperatures or very high strain rates where other deformation mechanisms could dominate
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvement in ductility is uncertain and depends on specific processing conditions such as the achieved grain size and exact modification of stacking fault energies; additional in-situ studies are required to precisely correlate microstructural changes to ductility gains

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare sets of copper samples: one set with conventional coarse grains and another with controlled, refined grains achieved through specific thermomechanical treatments. Subject both sets to standardized tensile tests at room temperature while monitoring in-situ dislocation activity using TEM or DIC techniques.
measurements: Uniform elongation (strain at which necking begins)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the refined-grain samples do not statistically show a significant improvement in uniform elongation and ductile behavior relative to the coarse-grained samples under identical test conditions, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations

Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract High entropy alloys based on 3d transition metals display rich and promising magnetic characteristics for various high-technology applications. Understanding their behavior at finite temperature is, however, limited by the incomplete experimental data for single-phase alloys. Here we use first-principles alloy theory to investigate the magnetic structure of polymorphic CoCrFeMnNi in the paramagnetic state by accounting for the longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature. In both face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures, the LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr and Ni. The impact of LSFs is demonstrated on the phase stability, stacking fault energy and the fcc-hcp interfacial energy. The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions. With increasing temperature, the stacking fault energy increases, suppressing the formation of stacking faults and nano-twins. Our predictions are consistent with recent experimental findings.

decision.trend: Early studies in high‐entropy and refractory alloys focused on modifying the microstructure—via phase tuning, heat treatment, or even high‐pressure processing—to overcome inherent brittleness and obtain reasonable ductility. As these works evolved, researchers turned their attention to understanding and controlling the fundamental deformation mechanisms in alloys. For example, in PMC6093928 the Cantor alloy (an FCC-based material) was studied using first‐principles methods to reveal how longitudinal spin fluctuations affect stacking fault energies and, by extension, the ease of dislocation glide. Thus, the trend moved from empirical processing routes (e.g., modifying phase fractions or introducing precipitates) to a more detailed atomistic and combined experimental/simulation picture that pinpoints factors—particularly the role of the stacking fault energy and the availability of multiple slip systems in FCC structures—as key to ductility.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress, there remains a gap in quantitatively linking the microstructural parameters (such as grain size, stacking fault energy, and dislocation dynamics) in canonical FCC metals (e.g., copper and aluminum) to their ductile behavior under ambient conditions. The precise mechanisms by which these FCC metals maximize ductility, compared with more complex multi‐phase alloys, are not fully dissected.
decision.lever: Implementing in-situ characterization (e.g., TEM/DIC) alongside atomistic simulations to systematically probe dislocation activities and measure stacking fault energies in prototype FCC metals like copper with controlled grain sizes
decision.why: This approach builds directly on the insights from FCC-based systems (as in PMC6093928) and the trend toward connecting atomistic mechanisms with macroscopic ductility. By doing so, it addresses the unresolved connection between controlled microstructural parameters and ductile performance in standard FCC metals, offering a clear pathway to designing materials that achieve high ductility and revealing the underlying mechanisms.
